text: Traditional access-control architectures are based on centralised identity providers, institution-specific authentication systems, and relatively static permission-management mechanisms. These approaches can provide effective access control within an organisational boundary, but they become difficult to apply when authorisation decisions involve multiple independent entities. In such settings, no single participant may possess sufficient authority to determine access independently, and trust cannot necessarily be assumed on the basis of membership in a common administrative domain. This problem is particularly relevant in healthcare, where data-sharing decisions may require the coordinated participation of patients, guardians, healthcare professionals, and institutional authorities [31, 9]. ⟦d⟧These scenarios demonstrate that authorisation is increasingly a distributed governance problem rather than simply a process of authenticating a user and checking a static permission⟦/d⟧⟦a⟧In these settings, authorisation is a distributed governance problem, not just a check of a user's login and a static permission⟦/a⟧ [29].

text: Problem Statement

Existing consent-management and decentralised access-control approaches represent authorisation through database records, access-control entries, smart contracts, or blockchain transactions. These mechanisms can improve record integrity, traceability, and auditability, but consent itself often remains a relatively passive artefact indicating that a permission or approval has been created [10, 13]. The relationship between the consent record, the identity of the participants, their authority to act, the applicable policy constraints, and the resulting access decision is frequently treated as separate technical concerns. Likewise, successful authentication establishes that an entity has been identified, but authentication does not automatically establish that the entity possesses the authority to access a particular patient's information. Even where identity and collective approval have been satisfied, an access request may still be inappropriate if it exceeds the authorised purpose or data scope. The requested operation must also be evaluated against the policy constraints associated with the consent.

text: Research Motivation

The motivation of this research is to develop a Trust Computing perspective in which trustworthy healthcare data access emerges from the coordinated verification and enforcement of multiple security conditions. Under this perspective, trust is not treated as a property that is provided by blockchain, decentralised identity, or any other individual technology. Instead, trustworthy authorisation is understood as an emergent property of a decision process in which independently verifiable conditions must be satisfied. Trusted Computing provides an additional perspective on the protection and verification of security-critical processes. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), for example, provide hardware-supported isolation that can protect sensitive computation from compromised or untrusted operating environments [23, 17]. Remote attestation mechanisms can further provide evidence concerning the integrity of the execution environment in which a security-sensitive process is performed. Nevertheless, Trusted Computing does not by itself determine the correctness of an authorisation policy. Consequently, secure execution and trustworthy authorisation address complementary rather than identical problems. Future work can therefore investigate how trusted execution and remote attestation can strengthen the enforcement and verification of decentralised consent decisions.

text: The current research concentrates on the foundational dimensions required to construct this trust-oriented authorisation model. The first focus is the development of a trust-centric consent representation capable of capturing the conditions associated with an authorisation decision. Building on this representation, the research investigates how decentralised identifiers and verifiable credentials can establish trustworthy participants while maintaining a clear conceptual separation between identity authentication and authorisation authority. The framework then extends individual trust to collective trust through a multi-party authorisation mechanism, ensuring that sensitive healthcare data access can require the coordinated approval of multiple independently verified participants. Finally, policy-aware access control is incorporated to ensure that a valid identity or sufficient set of approvals cannot be used to obtain information outside the purpose or data scope authorised by the patient. These four dimensions, RO1 to RO4, collectively define the foundational scope of Multi-Party Patient Consent. RO1 to RO4 are completed with validation and evaluation at the current stage. RO5 adds temporal validity and lifecycle trust, because trust cannot be regarded as permanently established at the moment a consent is created. A consent that was valid when initially approved may subsequently become invalid due to expiration, revocation, or a change in its authorised lifecycle state. RO6 concerns formal security assurance and empirical validation. RO5 and RO6 are in progress, and part of each has already been delivered. RO6 is partially completed through the implementation and initial scenario-based validation of the HALAH (History Access Link for Authorised Healthcare) prototype. For RO5, this prototype provides a lifecycle-aware consent mechanism capable of rejecting access after expiration or revocation. The remaining formal security assurance and comprehensive empirical evaluation will be conducted in the next stage.

text: Key Requirements for Trustworthy Multi-Party Consent Authorisation

Trustworthy access should be understood as an outcome of the coordinated satisfaction of multiple independently verifiable conditions. The six requirements below collectively establish a progression from consent modelling and participant trust to collective authorisation, policy enforcement, temporal and lifecycle control, and finally formal security assurance and empirical validation. Each matches one sub-research question (Section 3), and each sub-research question addresses a distinct dimension of the proposed trust-oriented healthcare authorisation framework.

items: **Req 1: Representation of consent as an evaluable authorisation object.** Rather than representing consent as a simple association between a patient, a requester, and a permission, consent should be represented as a structured and evaluable authorisation object. The object should incorporate identity information, authority requirements, policy constraints on purpose, data scope, and jurisdiction, temporal validity, and authorisation evidence so that a consent decision can be evaluated when a subsequent data-access request is made.

**Req 2: Decentralised verification of identity and authority.** Decentralised ⟦d⟧Identity (DID)⟦/d⟧⟦n⟧Identifiers (DIDs)⟦/n⟧ and Verifiable Credentials (VCs) provide an alternative to conventional identity architectures based exclusively on centralised identity providers. Participants should establish persistent and cryptographically verifiable identifiers without dependence on a single identity provider. Identity verification establishes who is participating, while authority verification determines whether that entity satisfies the requirements associated with a particular consent. This separation prevents successful authentication from being interpreted as automatic authorisation.

**Req 3: Multi-party authorisation through a verifiable threshold.** Multiple independently verified participants can jointly establish a trustworthy consent decision without allowing a single participant to unilaterally authorise sensitive healthcare data access. A predefined threshold of independent approvals from designated parties should be modelled as an explicit and independently verifiable security condition within the consent object.

**Req 4: Policy- and context-aware enforcement at the time of access.** A requester may possess a valid identity, valid credentials, and even the required multi-party approval while still requesting information outside the scope authorised by the patient. The access decision must also be evaluated against the purpose and data-scope constraints explicitly associated with the consent. Every request should be evaluated against contextual constraints such as jurisdiction, because many unauthorised disclosures are caused by legitimate requesters who exceed their scope [11].

**Req 5: Temporal validity and lifecycle control of consent.** A consent that has expired, has been revoked, or has entered an invalid state must not be treated as an active authorisation even when its original identity, authority, and approval conditions were valid. The requirement is to ensure that an authorisation remains valid only within its permitted time interval and lifecycle state, and that expiration, immediate and verifiable revocation, and unauthorised state transitions are correctly enforced at every request.

**Req 6: Verifiable auditability and security assurance.** A system may execute valid authorisation scenarios without demonstrating that invalid identities, insufficient approvals, or policy violations cannot produce an unintended access decision. Every decision should preserve verifiable evidence to explain the reason for that decision. Formal analysis or systematic adversarial testing should provide a complementary layer through which the expected security properties of the authorisation model can be explicitly defined and examined.

text: The eligibility criteria were defined before the screening process to ensure consistency in the selection of studies. text: Main Research Question

Based on the identified research gap, the overarching research question is formulated as follows: **"How can a trust-oriented computing framework establish and enforce trustworthy multi-party consent for decentralised healthcare data sharing under identity, authority, and policy constraints?"** The formulation of this question deliberately emphasises trust-oriented computing rather than any individual implementation technology. The terms establish and enforce represent two complementary aspects of the research problem. Establishment concerns how trustworthy participants, authority relationships, and collective consent decisions are created. Enforcement concerns how these established conditions are evaluated when a healthcare data-access request is made.

text: Research Questions as an Integrated Problem

The six sub-research questions are not independent technical questions. RQ1 establishes the conceptual object. RQ2 establishes the trustworthiness of the participants. RQ3 then extends this participant-level trust into a collective decision. RQ4 determines whether the resulting authorisation is applicable to the specific data-access request. RQ5 further introduces the dynamic dimension of trust by determining whether the authorisation remains valid with respect to its temporal conditions and lifecycle state. Finally, RQ6 establishes the assurance layer by formally defining the resulting security properties and empirically evaluating whether the implemented framework enforces them correctly. The integrated authorisation condition can therefore be expressed as {E22}. Here, V~I~ represents identity and authority validity, V~A~ collective authorisation validity, V~P~ policy and contextual compliance, V~T~ temporal validity, and V~L~ jurisdictional compliance, while the revocation and token states of the lifecycle are evaluated within V~A~ and its time-based states within V~T~.

text: RO1: Trust-Centric Consent Model

The first research objective is to develop a trust-aware consent model that represents patient consent as a structured and evaluable authorisation object. The model incorporates identity information, authority requirements, policy constraints, and authorisation evidence so that a consent decision can be evaluated when a subsequent data-access request is made. RO1 directly addresses RQ1 and establishes the conceptual foundation for the remaining objectives. It defines the information that must be represented before consent can be interpreted as an authorisation decision rather than merely as a static approval record.

text: RO2: Decentralised Identity and Authority Trust

The second research objective is to develop a decentralised identity and authority verification mechanism using decentralised identifiers and verifiable credentials. The objective is to establish trustworthy participants while explicitly separating identity authentication from authorisation authority. RO2 addresses RQ2 and provides the trust inputs required by the subsequent multi-party authorisation process. The objective is based on the principle that successful identity verification does not automatically imply permission to access healthcare data.

text: RO3: Trustworthy Multi-Party Authorisation

The third research objective is to develop a threshold-based multi-party authorisation mechanism through which multiple independently verified participants can jointly establish a trustworthy consent decision. The objective is to prevent unilateral authorisation where collective approval is required. The guardian set G, fixed at consent creation, defines which participants are eligible to contribute an approval to the authorisation process. Each participant must submit an approval that can be independently verified through EIP-712 signature recovery. Invalid approvals are rejected and must not contribute to the threshold count. A valid signature is required from every listed guardian, so the threshold equals |G|, an N-of-N condition demonstrated in the 2-of-2 configuration. In this case, one valid approval is insufficient, whereas two valid approvals satisfy the threshold. RO3 addresses RQ3 and extends the consent model from an individual permission statement to a collective authorisation decision.

text: RO4: Policy- and Context-Aware Access Control

The fourth research objective is to develop a policy-aware authorisation mechanism that evaluates the purpose and data scope of a requested operation against the constraints defined by the consent. The objective is to ensure that a valid identity and sufficient multi-party approval cannot be used to obtain healthcare information outside the authorised scope. A request is permitted only when the purpose is compatible with the consent and the requested data scope is a non-empty subset of the authorised EMR modules. In the current prototype, the request purpose is taken from the consent, so the purpose check confirms that the consent purpose is a supported healthcare use, while the comparison with a separately declared request purpose is left to the next stage. RO4 directly addresses RQ4 and completes the foundational authorisation model. Together, RO1–RO4 establish the representation, verification, collective authorisation, and policy-enforcement mechanisms required for a trust-oriented healthcare data-sharing decision.

text: RO5: Temporal and Lifecycle Trust

The fifth research objective is to extend the trust-oriented framework with temporal validity and consent lifecycle controls. The objective is to ensure that an authorisation remains valid only within its permitted time interval and lifecycle state, and that expiration, revocation, and unauthorised state transitions are correctly enforced. RO5 addresses RQ5 and extends the foundational authorisation model into a dynamic consent environment. The current HALAH code already collects a start time and expiry time during consent creation. The prototype records them on-chain as notBefore and expiry within the consent token, enforces the temporal validity window at every access decision through V~T~, implements end-to-end revocation, including an on-chain revoke transaction, and manages the consent through an explicit lifecycle state machine. A consent that has expired or been revoked must not remain usable merely because its original approval threshold was satisfied. The remaining work concerns ⟦n⟧the lifecycle transition check, a formal lifecycle model, and ⟦/n⟧hardening these controls and extending them to consent modification, delegation, and guardian-set changes.

text: Layered Architecture and Component Decomposition

At the highest level, the architecture consists of three complementary layers. The View Layer represents the interaction boundary with independent healthcare stakeholders. The Controller Layer represents the security decision and coordination boundary. The Model Layer represents the persistent trust, consent, policy, and authorisation state. {F6} illustrates the conceptual relationship among these layers. The protected healthcare data are deliberately positioned outside the three MVC layers as a protected resource whose access is mediated by the Controller rather than directly exposed to the View.

text: An action submitted through the View represents a request or claim rather than a trusted authorisation outcome. The Controller Layer constitutes the principal security enforcement boundary. It receives requests from the View and coordinates the evaluation of the relevant trust conditions. These include decentralised identity verification, credential and authority verification, multi-party approval evaluation, policy and data-scope evaluation, and final authorisation. The Controller also generates audit evidence associated with the resulting decision. Consequently, the Controller acts as the coordination point through which sensitive operations must pass before protected healthcare data can be accessed. The Model therefore provides the information required for the Controller to evaluate an access request, but the existence of a Model object does not itself imply that access is permitted. MVC was selected in preference to a purely on-chain design for two reasons. First, the authorisation decision must combine the identity, threshold, policy, temporal, and jurisdictional evaluation performed by the Controller with the anchoring of consent state on the blockchain. Second, each stakeholder interface can be replaced without altering the enforcement logic, so the trust predicates are evaluated independently of any particular user interface.

text: Trust Evaluation and Architectural Boundaries

The architectural layers cooperate through a controlled authorisation sequence rather than through unrestricted direct communication. A healthcare data-access request is not evaluated according to a single authentication event. As illustrated in {F8}, the Controller coordinates a sequence of trust predicates representing the conditions established by the sub-research questions. The first condition, V~I~(u), determines whether the requesting participant possesses valid identity and authority evidence. The second condition, V~A~(C), determines whether the required independently verified participants have collectively satisfied the authorisation threshold N. The third condition, V~P~(C, R), determines whether the requested operation complies with the consent policy, including purpose and data-scope restrictions. The fourth condition, V~T~(C, t), determines whether the consent remains valid at the time of the request. The fifth condition, V~L~(C, R), determines whether the jurisdiction of the request satisfies the recorded jurisdictional constraint of the consent. The revocation and token states of the lifecycle are evaluated within V~A~, and its time-based states within V~T~, rather than within V~L~. The integrated decision can therefore be expressed as {E22}.

RO1 addresses RQ1 by developing a trust-aware consent model that represents patient consent as a structured and evaluable authorisation object. The purpose of this objective is to establish a formal representation of what the patient intends to authorise, who is permitted to participate in the authorisation process, which healthcare data may be accessed, and under what conditions. Overview of Decentralised Identity and Authority Trust

RO2 addresses RQ2 by developing a decentralised identity and authority verification mechanism using Decentralised Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials. The objective is to establish trustworthy participants while separating identity authentication from authorisation authority. RO2 provides the trust inputs required by the subsequent multi-party authorisation process. The objective is based on the principle that successful identity verification does not automatically imply permission to access healthcare data. The central principle of RO2 is {E47}.

text: Identity and Authority Verification Workflow

The workflow begins when a participant attempts to participate in the consent process or requests access to healthcare data. The system resolves and verifies the participant's DID and then retrieves the associated VC. The credential is checked for validity and its claims are examined to determine whether the participant possesses the authority required by the consent. As shown in {F12}, the output of RO2 is not an access-grant decision. It is a verified identity and authority result that can be consumed by RO3 and RO4. This separation prevents a participant from obtaining access merely by presenting a valid identity credential.

text: Verification Model and Algorithm

The procedure establishes a verifiable relationship between the participant u, the identity information represented by the DID, the attributes contained in the associated VC, and the authority requirements specified by the consent object C. The system first resolves the decentralised identifier (DID) associated with participant u. The system verifies the DID document and whether the relevant cryptographic information, such as verification methods and public keys, can be trusted. The VC provides machine-verifiable claims, such as professional role, organisational affiliation, or delegated authority. In the target design, the credential can be considered valid only when VC~valid~ = Sig~VC~ ∧ Issuer~valid~ ∧ Subject~match~ ∧ Time~valid~. The system determines whether the credential was issued by an acceptable issuer, whether it refers to the current participant, whether its signature is valid, and whether the credential remains within its validity period. If any of these conditions fails, the verification process returns INVALID.

text: Realisation in the Prototype

RO2 has been completed at the conceptual and prototype level. The current implementation demonstrates the separation between participant identity and authorisation authority. A valid healthcare participant identity can be verified independently from the question of whether that participant is authorised to access a particular patient's data. V~I~ in the current prototype combines a structural DID and credential-format check with EIP-712 verification of the signature of each listed guardian, and its outcome is recorded in the audit ledger. The condition VC~valid~ therefore defines the target verification model rather than the behaviour presently exercised by the demonstration. The doctor is not independently authenticated at consent creation, because the doctor DID is checked for DID format only when the access decision is evaluated. Cryptographic DID resolution against a registry, cryptographic validation of verifiable credentials, and authentication of the requester are acknowledged limitations reserved for the next stage. text: Procedure for Threshold-Based Multi-Party Authorisation

The procedure determines whether a consent-defined authorisation requirement has received sufficient valid approvals from the designated participants. The system first retrieves the required participant set G associated with the consent object C. The system obtains the threshold value N, which specifies the minimum number of valid and distinct approvals required to activate the authorisation. The threshold must satisfy 1 ≤ N ≤ |G|. The threshold therefore determines how many eligible participants must independently approve the consent before the authorisation becomes active. The approval a is not considered valid until the identity and authority of the submitting participant have been verified. The verification process may invoke the DID and VC verification procedure described in {A2}. If the verification fails, the approval is classified as invalid. The system records the invalid approval event and returns DENY for that approval attempt.

RO4 – Policy- and Context-Aware Access Control
Status: Done

RO4 directly addresses RQ4 and completes the foundational authorisation model investigated during ⟦n⟧the ⟦/n⟧current stage. The objective is to ensure that an otherwise valid requester cannot access healthcare information outside the purpose and data scope authorised by the consent. RO4 develops a policy-aware access-control mechanism capable of evaluating purpose and data-scope constraints before an access decision is issued. The objective is based on the observation that a valid identity and sufficient approval do not necessarily imply that every requested operation is permitted. A doctor may be a legitimate participant and may possess a valid consent, but the requested data may exceed the authorised scope or the requested purpose may not match the purpose specified by the patient. ⟦n⟧Section 9.1 defines the scope and policy conditions, Section 9.2 shows the policy-aware access workflow, Section 9.3 gives the decision algorithm, Section 9.4 qualifies what the prototype checks, and Section 9.5 states the outcome of RO4.⟦/n⟧

{F15} presents the RO5 workflow, which evaluates the consent’s temporal interval, lifecycle state, and revocation status before the system proceeds with the remaining authorisation conditions. This design ensures that a consent is not treated as permanently valid after it has expired or entered a state that no longer permits access. Temporal conditions and lifecycle state are represented in the Model, while their validity is evaluated by the Controller before an access decision is produced. The Consent Engine evaluates V~T~ and V~L~ from the application record, whereas the independent verification tool reads checkValid and checkValidAt on the deployed contract, which stores the notBefore and expiry fields.

items: **Temporal validity.** At every access request, the system compares the current time t with the consent validity interval. This step prevents a consent from being used before its effective start time or after its expiration time. At consent creation, the expiry time must be later than the start time. These temporal attributes define the period during which the consent is potentially valid.

**On-chain revocation.** Revocation represents a deliberate termination of the previously granted consent and must therefore override an otherwise valid temporal interval. The patient's withdrawal is confirmed as a revoke transaction on Sepolia in block 11,771,307, after which the contract reports the token as no longer valid. The blockchain or token layer provides persistence, traceability, and evidence of the resulting state. For subsequent requests, the system explicitly checks whether consent object C has been revoked in the local store. If the state is not ACTIVE, the access request is denied, and the refusal is reported in the doctor interface rather than written to the audit ledger in the current prototype.

text: The Proposed Solution for RO6
RO6 – Formal Security Assurance and Empirical Validation
Status: Partially completed (for RQ1 to RQ4)

RO6 addresses RQ6 by formally analysing and empirically evaluating whether the proposed trust-oriented authorisation framework satisfies its defined security and authorisation properties. The objective combines two complementary forms of assurance. Formal security assurance specifies the conditions under which the authorisation mechanism should be considered secure and consistent. Empirical validation evaluates whether the implemented system behaves according to those conditions. Experimental success alone cannot establish that unauthorised access is impossible under the stated model, while formal reasoning establishes security properties only under explicitly defined assumptions. Consequently, the two forms of evidence are complementary rather than interchangeable. RO6 is partially completed through the implementation and scenario-based validation of the HALAH prototype for RQ1 to RQ4. text: **Scenario 2: guardian approval and activation (validates RQ2 and RQ3).** Rather than relying on a single approval authority, the procedure requires a predefined number of eligible participants to independently provide valid approvals. Each participant must submit an approval that can be independently verified. Each guardian approves the consent with an EIP-712 typed-data signature that binds the approval to this consent, to this guardian, and to the Sepolia network (chainId 11155111). The system recovers the signer address and compares it with the address associated with the guardian DID, so a signature produced for another consent, another guardian, or another chain is rejected. If the participant has already submitted a valid approval, the system rejects the additional approval. Invalid approvals are rejected and must not contribute to the threshold count. Valid approvals are recorded and the current approval count is updated. In the implemented configuration, N = |G|, so all eligible participants must independently approve the consent before the authorisation becomes active. In this case, one valid approval is insufficient, whereas two valid approvals satisfy the threshold condition of Section 8. This mechanism allows the framework to distinguish between insufficient and sufficient collective authorisation. The prototype demonstrates that a consent object remains unable to establish valid authorisation until the required number of independently verified participants has approved it. When the threshold is reached, the implementation assigns an SBT identifier and records the corresponding minting event, and the anchoring starts in the background, as shown in {F23}. ⟦b⟧The public anchoring of the evaluated consent f050c29a in block 11,771,243 (block 11,771,581 for consent 04da25f5 in {F23})⟦/b⟧ provides an immutable or otherwise tamper-evident record of the transition from a pending consent state to an active authorisation state. The trust decision is established by the verification of participants and the satisfaction of the authorisation threshold.

text: **Scenario 3: authorised doctor access (validates RQ4).** The Doctor interface retrieves a consent, evaluates its state, allows a requested scope to be selected from the consent scope, generates a proof, checks the requested scope, and invokes the authorisation function before returning data. As shown in {F27}, the decision matrix enables validation results to be traced from the final decision back to the individual authorisation conditions that produced that decision. A request is permitted only when the consent purpose is a supported healthcare use and the requested data scope is non-empty and contained within the authorised scope. Consequently, a valid identity and sufficient multi-party approval are necessary but not sufficient conditions for access. Here, the system generates or verifies the evidence supporting the access decision as a Groth16 zero-knowledge proof. Because the prover and the verifier run on the same server, the proof demonstrates the integration of the zero-knowledge toolchain rather than an additional privacy guarantee. As shown in {F29}, once the request has been successfully authorised, the system retrieves only the healthcare data satisfying the authorised scope and displays them per EMR module. This rule prevents a legitimate participant from obtaining data outside the patient’s authorised scope.

text: **Scenario 5: revocation followed by refusal (validates the revocation control of RQ5).** Revocation should invalidate a previously established consent rather than merely create a new record indicating that the consent has changed. The patient revokes the evaluated consent, the system submits a revoke transaction to the contract, and the consent is displayed as REVOKED with its token number. A subsequent request by the doctor ⟦d⟧fails at V~A~, because the system verifies that the consent has not been revoked or otherwise transitioned into an inactive state.⟦/d⟧⟦n⟧is refused by the doctor subsystem at the consent-state check, because the consent is no longer ACTIVE; the V~A~ predicate itself rejects a revoked consent, which test A8 exercises.⟦/n⟧ Revocation represents a deliberate termination of the previously granted consent and must therefore override an otherwise valid temporal interval. items: **Formal assurance.** The formal component will specify and analyse the security properties, consistency requirements, and soundness conditions of the trust-oriented authorisation mechanism. The soundness property Decision(C, R, t) = ALLOW ⇒ V~I~ ∧ V~A~ ∧ V~P~ ∧ V~T~ ∧ V~L~ and the lifecycle invariant of Section 10 will be verified by model checking of the state machine or by proof over the predicate definitions. Formal analysis will be used to reason about whether unauthorised entities or invalid authorisation conditions can produce an apparently valid access decision under defined assumptions, and every property must be either verified or refuted by an explicit counterexample.

**Full performance and scalability study.** The preliminary measurements will be repeated over a larger number of consents, guardians, and access requests, and the end-to-end decision latency will be measured under concurrent load.
